paper_title: Tree-Ising: Repairing Language Models with Bit-Level Ising Edits

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Weight-space programming, introduced in recent MIT work by Takehi et al., enables a frontier LLM agent to read a network's weights and write a repair. Their GPT-6 Astra agent corrected the reasoning loops of Qwen3.5-0.8B without gradients, using 158 agent turns, 89.7 million tokens, and 50 forward-pass requests. Our method, Tree-Ising, casts this repair as a sparse discrete optimization problem over the model's own BF16 weights. Forward statistics define an objective that weakens a loop direction, strengthens a concluding direction, and preserves the layer's output on productive tokens. Within a state-tree representation, where lossless BF16 storage acts as a special case, the admissible edits are sign flips and exponent shifts that preserve all shared group exponents and mantissas. We decompose this objective exactly into independent QUBO (Ising) problems, one per output row, which we solve on a GPU using simulated annealing or quantum-inspired simulated bifurcation. On the agent's two layers, Tree-Ising achieves 54.6% on MATH-500, outperforming the agent's edit (51.7%) under the same evaluation protocol, while the base model scores 7.9% as reported. The simulated bifurcation solver yields a statistically indistinguishable repair at 55.1%. Both solvers outperform the agent edit across all five math benchmarks, with statistically significant improvements on MATH-500 and GSM8K after correcting for multiple comparisons. Our approach modifies 13% to 17% fewer weights and reduces BF16 bit flips by a factor of 2.2 to 2.3. It requires only four forward-pass requests and zero LLM tokens, with the annealing recipe costing about $0.90 in GPU time. On Qwen3.5-2B, with layers and dose selected using only the base model, the same recipe increases greedy GSM8K accuracy from 21.6% to 69.4%. As a proof of concept, we execute an eight-variable repair subproblem using QAOA on an IBM Heron processor.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Weight-space programming has recently emerged as compelling paradigm in model editing. Takehi et al. [55] at MIT investigated whether language model can program the weights of another network: reading its parameters, diagnosing 1 TREE-ISING Bit-level Ising edits for model repair failure, and writing fix directly into the weights, with an LLM agent acting as the programmer. Their most prominent demonstration targets common failure mode in small reasoning models. In thinking mode, Qwen3.5-0.8B frequently falls into short cycle of repeated text, continuing until the token budget is exhausted; this occurs on 93% of MATH-500 problems under 32,768-token cap, limiting its accuracy to merely 7.9%. GPT-6 Astra agent, provided with the checkpoint, practice problems, and budget of 50 forward-pass requests, traced these loops to the MLPs of layers 15 and 19 and rewrote 64 columns in each of their output projections. Consequently, MATH-500 accuracy rose to 48.1% without single gradient step. While this result proves that weights can be programmed, it also highlights the substantial price of doing so with an agent: 158 turns, 89.7 million tokens from frontier model, 50 forward-pass requests, and 15.6 hours of compute for single edit  (Table 4)  . Crucially, every step of this process relies on judgment calls made in natural language, offering no guarantee that the resulting edit is the optimal one available. In this work, we cast the repair as sparse discrete optimization problem over the stored weights. The evidence gathered by the agentforward passes on looping answers versus successful onescan be formalized as mathematical objective, where an edit is defined as discrete choice among changes to stored bits. We build this formulation on state trees [3], general representation of neural networks in which every weight is path of discrete decisions through tree, and weights sharing the same decision share the recording node. Lossless BF16 storage is special case of this representation, where each group of 64 weights shares its exponent as node; this is the specific case we utilize. Our formulation, which we call TREE-ISING, comprises five key steps (Figure 2): 1. Represent the weights as state trees. In the lossless BF16 state tree, multiplying weight by power of two or flipping its sign alters only its 4-bit state and sign bit. Moves that preserve each groups maximum leave the shared exponent untouched. Preselecting one such move per candidate weight reduces the edit to series of binary decisions. 2. Select the layers. single forward scan of the base model evaluates how strongly each MLP writes along the loop direction, automatically identifying the layers to edit without requiring an agent. 3. Define the objective. Forward statistics yield loop direction and concluding direction. The objective is to minimize the layers projection along their combination on loop tokens, preserve the output on productive tokens, and restrict the total number of modified weights. 4. Formulate as an Ising model. For fixed statistics and preselected moves, the objective decomposes exactly into independent subproblems, one per output row. Each row subproblem is formulated as dense QUBO, equivalently an Ising model. 5. Solve the optimization. GPU solves all row problems for given layer simultaneously using simulated annealing or simulated bifurcation, quantum-inspired Ising solver. Because these are native Ising models, they also map directly onto quantum annealers and QAOA. Evaluated on the two layers targeted by the agent, TREE-ISING achieves 54.6% on MATH-500, outperforming the agents edit (51.7%) under an identical evaluation protocol, while the base model scores only 7.9% in the evaluation of Takehi et al. [55]. Notably, it outperforms the agent edit across all five math benchmarks tested, with statistically significant gains on MATH-500 and GSM8K after correcting for multiple comparisons (Tables 1 and 3). Furthermore, replacing the annealer with simulated bifurcation [17, 18] yields an equally effective repair, achieving 55.1% on MATH-500 with 4% fewer modified weights, demonstrating that the results do not hinge on single solver. Crucially, this approach requires only 4 forward-pass requests instead of 50, reducing forward-pass compute by factor of 34 and eliminating the need for LLM tokens entirely. The entire recipe executes in 31 minutes at cost of approximately $0.90. Moreover, the resulting edit is substantially smaller: it modifies 13% fewer weights, reduces BF16 bit flips by factor of 2.2, cuts state-tree bit changes by factor of 4, and, by construction of its move set, leaves all shared exponents and mantissas untouched. It is important to clarify the scope of this comparison. The agent incurred significant cost to discover the failure, identify the direction, and select the layers. In contrast, our recipe was designed after analyzing its public logs; on Qwen3.5-0.8B, it reuses the agents two selected layers and calibrates its dose based on the agents edit. Thus, the cost figures compare the exhaustive process of finding fix against the application of fixed, optimized recipe. Our primary aim is to achieve superior repair through fewer weight modifications. For context, dense closed-form solution of the same objective, without sparsity or discrete moves, reaches similar accuracy on our practice screen but modifies 96% of the weights in both matrices62 times as many as TREE-ISING (Section 4.5). sections.title: 2 Background
sections.content: Reasoning loops. We define an answer as cut when the generation process reaches the maximum token budget before the model produces its final conclusion. In the models evaluated in this work, nearly all cut answers exhibit looping behavior: within the final 2,000 tokens, the majority of 8-grams have already appeared earlier in the same sequence. While repetition in neural text generation has been extensively studied through decoding heuristics and modified training objectives [22, 58, 59], and recent reports on reasoning models analyze how extended thinking traces interact with decoding configurations [12, 48], we frame looping as property of the networks weights. This perspective treats the failure mode as an artifact that direct weight edit can resolve. Weight-space programming. Takehi et al. [55] enabled frontier LLM agent to read the parameters of Qwen3.5-0.8B and execute forward passes on practice problems. (2) One forward scan of the base model scores each MLPs write along the loop direction and selects layers 15 and 19 (Figure 3). The comprehensive logs released by the authors [54] detail every interaction, token count, and forward pass, allowing us to precisely quantify the computational cost of the procedure (Section 4.3). We denote the resulting checkpoint as the agent edit. Crucially, the agents workflow encompasses three distinct phases, which our formulation renders mathematically explicit: identifying the target layers, defining the optimization objective, and searching for the precise weight modifications required to achieve it.

We cast this edit as discrete optimization problem comprising five key steps (Figure 2): representing the weights and admissible moves (Section 3.1), selecting the target layers (Section 3.2), defining the optimization objective (Section 3.3), formulating the problem as independent Ising models (Section 3.4), and solving them (Section 3.5).

sections.title: 3.1 Step 1: a QUBO-friendly representation of the weights
sections.content: State trees. State trees [3] provide general representation for neural networks. Every weight is defined as path of discrete decisions from the root of tree to leaf, and weights that share the same decision share the node that records it. This representation seamlessly unifies low-bit compression and exact storage. Lossless BF16 storage is specific instance of this framework, and it is the one we employ. BF16 number consists of one sign bit, an 8-bit exponent e, and 7-bit mantissa [31]. The lossless BF16 state tree groups 64 consecutive weights within row and stores their maximum exponent once as shared node. Each individual weight then stores 4-bit state = {0, . . . , 14} and leaf containing its sign and mantissa; state 15 designates rare escape whose exponent is maintained in side list. This instantiation reproduces every weight exactly, cleanly separating what group shares (its exponent) from what each weight owns (its offset, sign, and mantissa), mirroring the structure of block floating-point and microscaling formats in their lossy counterparts [13, 51]. Because every stored quantity is discrete decision, an edit is fundamentally change of decisions. Tree-local moves. For standard weight with state D, factor with = log2 shifts the state to and flips the sign if < 0. move is deemed admissible only if it preserves the groups shared exponent and generates no escape. Growth (k > 0) requires k, ensuring no weight exceeds the group maximum; shrinkage (k < 0) requires 1 and 14, guaranteeing that the group maximum is never reduced and no weight falls outside the 4-bit range. Sign flips are universally admissible. Every admissible move is exact in BF16, preserves the mantissa, and alters at most the sign bit and the 4-bit state of single weight. For instance, the weight 0.125 in group with = 127 has = 3; doubling it yields 0.25 with = 2, resulting in change to single stored bit. Binary formulation and the role of the state tree. The binary nature of the formulation arises from preselecting one move per candidate weight (Section 3.4): the sole remaining decision is whether to apply it, rendering the edit vector of binary variables where every subsequent quantity is polynomial of degree at most two, conforming to the QUBO format. Multiplying by power of two is also exact in standard BF16, meaning the tree itself does not create the binary structure. Rather, its contribution lies in providing format-native move set and its corresponding accounting. Because admissible moves never alter the group maximum, the shared node is never rewritten, and the number of stored bits modified by an edit can be directly read from the tree. The guarantee that the edit writes no shared exponent and no mantissa therefore holds by construction, rather than as an empirical observation.

sections.title: 3.5 Step 5: solving
sections.content: GPU annealing. Our default solver processes all rows of given layer as single GPU batch via simulated annealing [33]. The final solve executes 16 replicas per row, starting from the zero edit, for 300 sweeps of single-spin Metropolis updates in random order. The temperature decreases geometrically from 2 to 104 times the rows median ha, and we retain the lowest-energy replica. Simulated bifurcation. As an alternative solver, we employ discrete simulated bifurcation (dSB) [17, 18], quantuminspired method that integrates the classical dynamics of coupled bifurcating oscillators and reads spins from their signs. Each replica initializes near the zero edit; the pump ramps up over the first quarter of 1,200 steps of size 0.5, and the best sampled state of every trajectory, refined by single-flip descent in float64, is retained. Rows are processed in batches of 32, maintaining the same replica counts as in annealing. All other components, including the candidates, the preselected moves, and the calibration protocol, remain unchanged, ensuring the two solvers differ solely in how each row problem is searched. Calibration. Two global scalars are calibrated prior to solving the individual row problems. The sparsity weight initializes at λ0 = 2 medianCP, δ 2, representing the median single-weight collateral over the retained weights and the three basic moves {1, 2, 1 2 }; the candidate moves themselves always utilize all eight factors. At each value of λ , geometric bisection over γ [106, 106], utilizing quick solves of 4 replicas and 60 sweeps, identifies the smallest γ whose edit reaches the target dose, and the final solve adopts that γ. If the layer subsequently exceeds its budget, λ is doubled and the γ search is repeated for at most six attempts, ensuring the dose target is re-met after every adjustment to λ . The statistics remain fixed throughout this process. Table 9 reports the achieved dose and edit count for every edited layer. Alternative solvers. Crucially, the formulation in Steps 1 through 4 is entirely solver-agnostic. The row problems are standard Ising models and can be seamlessly handed to any Ising solver, ranging from greedy descent to quantum annealing [28, 30] or QAOA [15]. We examine the quantum route in Section 6. 7 TREE-ISING Bit-level Ising edits for model repair

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Model and Edit. We apply our method to the down_proj matrices (1,024 3,584) in layers 15 and 19 of Qwen3.50.8B [48], matching the layers targeted by the agent edit. We configure the optimization with = 512 candidates per row, β = 0.5, and strict budget of 65,536 changed weights per layer. The target dose is set to 1.6 times the dose of the agent edit along the direction u, corresponding to targets of 6.7 and 6.1 times the layers own write for layers 15 and 19, respectively (Section 3.3); consequently, the two edits are not strictly dose-matched. Notably, the forward scan detailed in Section 3.2 selects these exact same two layers. However, the exclusion rule for this scan was finalized after observing the initial scores, and the entire recipe was designed retrospectively by analyzing the agents public logs. We refer to this specific configuration as the TREE-ISING edit. Unless otherwise specified, this edit utilizes the simulated annealing solver; variants marked with "SB" denote the identical recipe solved via simulated bifurcation (Section 3.5). complete list of hyperparameters and settings is provided in Section A. Data. The forward statistics are derived from 384 practice problems released alongside the agents evaluation harness, comprising 192 problems from the MATH training split and 192 from the GSM8K training split [6, 21]. An additional 128 held-out practice problems constitute the selection screen used for the ablation studies in Section 4.5. We note that early exploratory variants were evaluated on fixed subset of 100 MATH-500 problems; consequently, the full MATH-500 results include problems encountered during the development phase, limitation we address in Section 8. Evaluation. We strictly adhere to the evaluation protocol established by the agents authors [54]: generation is performed using vLLM [35] in thinking mode, with temperature of 0.6, top-p of 0.95, top-k of 20, presence penalty of 1.5, and maximum of 32,768 new tokens. The final boxed answer following the </think> token is graded using Math-Verify [36]. We report performance across five benchmarks: MATH-500 [39], GSM8K [6], AMC23 [1], Minerva Math [37], and OlympiadBench [20]. The suffix @k denotes the number of completions generated per problem, with accuracy defined as the mean correctness across these completions. To ensure fair comparison, both edited checkpoints are evaluated within the identical harness using the same random seeds, and paired statistical tests are conducted on problem-by-problem basis.

sections.title: 4.2 Accuracy and Termination
sections.content: Table 3 presents direct comparison of the edits. Crucially, with either solver, TREE-ISING outperforms the agent edit across all five benchmarks. The performance gains on MATH-500 (with four completions per problem) and on GSM8K remain statistically significant even after applying Bonferroni correction across all twelve comparisons with the agent edit (two solvers, six settings; < 0.05/12 in all four cases). Furthermore, with simulated annealing, the improvement on OlympiadBench is nominally significant (p = 0.045), though it does not survive the strict correction. The remaining differences fall within the expected noise margin. Two key observations clarify the evaluation harness. sections.title: 5 Transfer to Qwen3.5-2B Without a Reference Edit
sections.content: In our evaluation of Qwen3.5-0.8B, TREE-ISING relied on the agents selected layers and calibrated its dose based on the agents final edit. In this section, we eliminate both dependencies. We apply the method to novel model, autonomously selecting its target layers via the forward scan and calibrating the dose using the base-model rule defined in Section 3.3, while leaving the remainder of the recipe entirely unchanged. The Failure Mode. Qwen3.5-2B [49] comprises 24 layers with down_proj matrices of dimensions 2,048 6,144. Under greedy decoding (temperature 0, thinking mode, 8,192-token cap), the base model correctly answers only 21.6% of the 1,319 GSM8K test problems  (Table 7)  . The underlying cause mirrors the failure observed in the smaller model: 77.9% of its generations reach the token cap, and 1,018 of these 1,028 truncated answers exhibit looping behavior. Crucially, when the model does successfully terminate, it provides the correct answer 97.9% of the time. This indicates that the model possesses the requisite problem-solving capability but fails to halt its reasoning. We specifically selected greedy decoding for this evaluation because an initial probe on 200 GSM8K test problems revealed that the base model struggles most severely under these conditions; consequently, the recipe has not yet been evaluated under the models recommended sampling settings or on the MATH-500 benchmark. The Recipe. We first prompt the base model to answer the same 384 practice problems using greedy decoding, yielding 16.9% success rate with 83.1% of the answers truncated. The forward scan subsequently ranks layers 23, 19, 15, and 14 highest (Figure 3, bottom). Applying our exclusion rule for the final layer isolates layers 15 and 19, precisely matching the pair selected for the smaller model. The forward statistics are derived from 275 looping and 65 correct traces. We set the target dose to 6.5 times each layers own write, and allocate budget of 200,000 changed weights per layer, representing approximately 1.6% of single matrix and closely aligning with the 1.8% utilized for the smaller model. All remaining hyperparameters are identical to those detailed in Section 4. The entire pipeline, encompassing the layer scan and single validation screen, executes in just 26 minutes on single A100 GPU. Crucially, this process requires no LLM agent, no reference checkpoint, and no gradient computations. Results. Applying the unchanged recipe elevates GSM8K accuracy from 21.6% to 69.4%, representing substantial gain of 47.8 percentage points  (Table 7)  . The edit successfully solves 669 problems that the base model fails to answer, while incorrectly altering the solution for 38 of the 285 problems the base model originally solved correctly (a 13% degradation on those specific instances). Notably, when evaluated on the 1,119 problems outside the initial 200-problem probe used to select the decoding setting, the performance remains consistent: 69.6% accuracy versus 21.6% for the base model (571 problems solved exclusively by the edit, 34 exclusively by the base model, and 208 by both). Furthermore, the proportion of truncated answers drops precipitously from 77.9% to 26.7%. While the accuracy on fully completed answers decreases slightly from 97.9% to 94.7%, it is important to note that these figures refer to different subsets of problems; the 38 lost problems confirm that the edit does perturb some correct base-model trajectories. sections.title: 6 Quantum-Hardware Proof of Concept
sections.content: We report small proof of concept for executing repair-derived Ising objective on an IBM Heron quantum processor using the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) [15, 61]. This specific instance isolates eight candidate weights from single row of layer 15 in Qwen3.5-0.8B, with all other variables in the row fixed to zero. The separately calibrated parameter γ = 0.0844 adheres to single-weight threshold rule, and we set λ = λ0 (Section B). With eight binary variables yielding 28 = 256 possible assignments, exhaustive enumeration establishes the exact optimum at negligible computational cost. We optimized the QAOA angles classically using exact statevector simulation. In single hardware execution, the depth-two QAOA circuit sampled the optimum in 110 out of 1,024 shots, compared to merely four shots for uniform control. We note that uniform sampling serves as relatively weak baseline for assessing optimization performance; matched random-angle circuits and classical solvers applied to identical instances would provide more rigorous comparison. Full circuit configurations, sampling results, and resource accounting are detailed in Section B. Crucially, this experiment establishes that small, separately calibrated instance can be successfully encoded, executed, and sampled on quantum hardware. However, it does not constitute evidence of quantum advantage. As demonstrated in Section 4, simulated annealing, simulated bifurcation, and the closed-form continuous edit all yield statistically indistinguishable accuracy, indicating that the current row-level problems are not computationally challenging for classical solvers, nor do marginal improvements in row energy translate to superior model performance. The primary value of these problems for quantum optimization lies in their role as source of structured, real-world Ising instances equipped with meaningful downstream metric: the accuracy of the repaired model. Significantly harder formulations, such as joint move selection or explicit bit budgets (Section C), would be required before quantum solver could offer tangible advantage. Consequently, the full-model accuracy results reported in Sections 4 and 5 are derived entirely from the classical GPU solver. subsequent investigation into hybrid refinement would condition each block on the GPU solution, apply the established repair calibration, and evaluate the resulting checkpoint on standard benchmarks. 13 TREE-ISING Bit-level Ising edits for model repair

sections.title: 7 Related work
sections.content: Weight-space programming and model editing. Takehi et al. [55] investigated whether general-purpose LLM can read and write network weights; among other tasks, their agent successfully repairs the reasoning loops of Qwen3.5-0.8B. We study the identical repair task but replace the LLM agent with an optimizer built from the same empirical evidence. Classical model editing typically modifies factual associations through targeted updates of MLP weights [41, 42], locates knowledge within individual neurons [11], learns editors that predict weight updates [43], or combines fine-tuning differences [27]. Crucially, these methods produce continuous updates. In contrast, TREE-ISING selects sparse, discrete changes that the stored weight format can represent exactly, and Section 4.5 compares our approach with ROME-like rank-one solution of our own objective. Furthermore, while bit-flip attacks demonstrate that few flipped bits can substantially alter networks behavior [50], we leverage this same sensitivity to repair rather than to harm. Activation steering and directional interventions. Steering methods typically add directions to the residual stream at inference time [38, 56, 62], and directional ablation can be folded directly into the weights [5]. Our directions are contrasts of the same kind, measured at the onset of loops and at the conclusion of successful thinking traces. However, our intervention takes the form of sparse weight edit optimized against collateral penalty, requiring no modifications at inference time. Mechanistic studies of transformer circuits strongly motivate reading such directions directly from the residual stream [14]. Closest to our setting, ThinkEdit [53] identifies linear direction governing reasoning length, isolates small set of attention heads driving overly short reasoning, and removes that direction from their output projections, altering approximately 0.2% of the parameters. We address the opposite failure modereasoning that never terminatesand edit MLP output projections through sparse discrete moves rather than continuous projection. Repetition and looping. Degenerate repetition has been extensively addressed through decoding heuristics [22] and modified training objectives [58, 59], and recent reports on reasoning models analyze how extended thinking traces interact with decoding configurations [12, 48]. In contrast, TREE-ISING alters neither the decoder nor the training process; it simply edits the weights once, entirely offline. Weight formats. Block floating-point and microscaling formats share exponents within groups of weights [13, 51], and lossless BF16 compression exploits the low entropy of these exponents [60]. State trees [3] provide general representation of neural networks as paths of shared discrete decisions, with lossless BF16 storage and low-bit compression serving as specific instances; that work also heals compressed model using gradient and curvature estimates. In our formulation, the state tree fundamentally defines the admissible moves of forward-only objective. QUBO formulations of network weights. AdaRound derives binary rounding problem from second-order approximation of the task loss [46], and Muñiz Subiñas et al. [45] formulate layer-output reconstruction for quantization as an exact QUBO that separates into independent output rows, solving it via simulated annealing. Layer-output reconstruction also underpins many pruning and quantization methods [16, 19]. Our objective augments this reconstruction term with behavioral term along measured direction and sparsity cost, operating over moves that preserve the stored format intact. Formulated as Ising models, these row problems connect seamlessly to the broad toolbox of Ising formulations [40], simulated annealing [33], quantum annealing [28, 30], QAOA [15], and digital or analogue Ising machines [17, 44]. Quantum hardware for neural networks and LLMs. Quantum annealers have been utilized to train binary neural networks [52] and to select pruning and quantization configurations for convolutional networks [57]. For LLMs, recent work integrates variational quantum circuits into pretrained model, either as parameter-efficient fine-tuning modules executed on superconducting processor [34] or as unitary adapters inside the projection layers of Llama 3.1 8B running on IBM hardware [2]. In those studies, the quantum circuit constitutes novel addition to the model architecture. In TREE-ISING, however, the model form remains entirely unchanged: the quantum device, much like the GPU, simply solves for which of the models existing BF16 weights should be modified, as demonstrated here on single eight-variable subproblem. 14 TREE-ISING Bit-level Ising edits for model repair

sections.title: 8 Limitations
sections.content: Scope. Our study addresses single failure mode: reasoning loops, specifically within two models of single family that share hybrid linear/full-attention architecture, evaluated exclusively on mathematical benchmarks. We have not assessed instruction-following capabilities, although Takehi et al. [55] report that the agent edit raised IFEval from 21.0% to 62.3%, nor have we tested general language modeling or non-mathematical benchmarks. Consequently, side effects remain unmeasured beyond the collateral term, which protects the layers output only on tokens derived from the practice problems. Evaluating larger models, alternative model families, and other behavioral failure modes remains direction for future work. Baselines and Evaluation. The base models 7.9% accuracy on MATH-500 is the figure reported by Takehi et al. [55]; we did not independently rerun the base model in our evaluation harness. Furthermore, the continuous edits detailed in Section 4.5 were evaluated exclusively on the 128-problem practice screen. Early exploratory variants on Qwen3.5-0.8B were screened on 100 MATH-500 problems, meaning the full MATH-500 results include problems exposed during development; however, the performance gap remains consistent on the 400 strictly held-out problems (Section 4.2). Each benchmark evaluation utilized single generation seed. The p-values reported in the tables are nominal; notably, only the gains on MATH-500@4 and GSM8K over the agent edit survive strict Bonferroni correction across the twelve agent comparisons. Design Choices. Our repair recipe was formulated retrospectively after analyzing the agents public logs. On Qwen3.5-0.8B, the edit utilizes the agents selected layers and dose 1.6 times that of the agents, calibrated on the practice screen; notably, no strictly dose-matched edit was executed. While the Qwen3.5-2B experiment eliminates both of these dependencies, the rule excluding the final layer was established after inspecting the 0.8B scan. Furthermore, the layers selected in both models are full-attention blocks, suggesting that this agreement may stem from their shared architectural design rather than independent validation. For Qwen3.5-2B, greedy decoding and the GSM8K benchmark were selected based on base-model results from 200-problem GSM8K test subset where the base model struggles most, whereas all edit-specific settings were determined solely on the practice problems. Surrogate Objective and Solvers. Our objective functions as first-order surrogate derived from the statistics of the unedited model: it inherently ignores how an edit in one layer alters the inputs to subsequent layers, and the dose serves merely as linear proxy for the desired behavioral shift. What remains mathematically exact is the decomposition of this surrogate into independent row problems once candidate columns and single move per weight are fixed; however, these two choices, along with the row solvers themselves, are heuristic. The practice screen resolves performance differences of approximately four percentage points, leaving the optimal dose and move set somewhat uncertain. Each solver was executed only once with single seed, and their run times were not measured under strictly matched conditions; therefore, we make no definitive claims regarding their relative computational speed. Accounting. Our state-tree bit counts assume straightforward encoder and deliberately exclude modifications within the payloads of existing escapes; furthermore, direct patching of compressed checkpoint has not yet been implemented. The reported time and cost metrics cover single execution of fixed recipe at list prices and explicitly exclude method development costs on both sides. Stage timings are derived from single runs executed with two versions of the solver script and should not be interpreted as rigorous scaling measurement. Quantum Hardware. The quantum hardware evaluation is confined to single eight-variable subproblem, encompassing just 8 of the 7.3 million weights across the two edited matrices, with the remainder of its row fixed to zero. This evaluation utilized dose calibration declared separately from the published edit, angles optimized classically, single hardware job, and one calibration period. Crucially, the resulting solution was not written back into model. The control baseline sampled uniformly; random-angle control on the identical compiled circuits has not been executed. Consequently, this result demonstrates correct mapping and objective-consistent sampling on quantum hardware, not computational advantage over classical solvers. Furthermore, Equation (14) bounds the theoretical benefit of any faster solver within the confines of our current recipe. 15 TREE-ISING Bit-level Ising edits for model repair

sections.title: 9 Conclusion
sections.content: While frontier LLM can repair looping model by directly editing its weights, we have demonstrated that this same repair task can be formulated as sparse discrete optimization problem and solved in matter of minutes. Specifically, TREE-ISING restricts admissible edits to sign flips and exponent shifts within the state tree of each weight group, evaluates them using forward statistics, and efficiently solves one small Ising problem per output row. On Qwen3.5-0.8B, our method produces an edit that is more accurate than the agents baseline while modifying fewer weights and far fewer bits, all for computational cost of approximately $0.90 per run. Crucially, both simulated annealing and the quantum-inspired simulated bifurcation solver yield repairs of equivalent quality, demonstrating that the performance gains stem fundamentally from the mathematical formulation itself rather than the tuning of specific solver. In contrast, dense closed-form solution of the identical objective achieves comparable accuracy only by altering nearly every weight across both matrices. Furthermore, when applied to Qwen3.5-2Bwith target layers and dosage calibrated entirely from the base modelthis same recipe elevates GSM8K accuracy under greedy decoding from 21.6% to 69.4%. Finally, an eight-variable QAOA experiment executed on IBM quantum hardware serves as preliminary proof of concept for running repair-derived Ising instance on quantum processor. Extending this validation to full-layer repairs and rigorously measuring the resulting downstream model accuracy remains compelling direction for future work. Code Availability. The source code implementing TREE-ISING will be made publicly available shortly at https: //github.com/TheQuantumGOAT/Tree-Ising.

sections.title: C Formulation extensions
sections.content: The results in this paper use the single-move formulation of Section 3.4. This appendix records three extensions that enlarge the optimization problem, and with it the potential role of specialized solvers. Joint choice among moves.
